theory.intro: A sample is **representative** when it accurately reflects the composition of the target population. An unrepresentative sample is biased because some subgroups are systematically over-represented or under-represented.
facts: **Sampling frame undercoverage** occurs when the selection list excludes part of the target population.
**Convenience bias** occurs when choosing easily reached people over-represents that specific group and excludes others.
**Volunteer bias** occurs when participants choose to respond, over-representing individuals with strong opinions.
An extremely **small sample size** fails to capture the natural variation of a large population.
In **stratified sampling**, a representative sample selects members from each subgroup in exact proportion to the population.
A **simple random sample** from a complete population list gives every member an equal chance of selection.

foundation.question_text: A researcher investigates the average weekly exercise hours of all adults in a town by surveying people exiting a gymnasium on Saturday morning. Decide whether the sample is representative and name the over-represented group.
foundation.solution_text:
Gym attendees are far more active than the general adult population.
Not representative; gym members are heavily over-represented while sedentary adults are excluded.

foundation.question_text: A radio host asks listeners to text in whether they support higher tolls on the harbour bridge. $1500$ listeners text in. Decide whether the sample is representative and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Listeners choose whether to participate, meaning only those who listen to that station and feel strongly about tolls will respond.
Not representative; self-selection over-represents vocal listeners with strong opinions.

foundation.question_text: To estimate the proportion of voters in a state of $4\,000\,000$ people who support a new policy, a pollster randomly selects $5$ voters. Decide whether this sample is representative and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
A sample of 5 is far too small to capture the diverse views of 4 million voters, and a single unusual response swings the estimate by $20\%$.
Not representative; the sample size is too small to be reliable.

foundation.question_text: A high school has $800$ students. The principal assigns every student a number from $1$ to $800$ and uses a computer random number generator to select $100$ students for a survey on school facilities. Decide whether this sample is representative and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Every student in the population has an equal and independent chance of being selected from the complete school roll.
Representative; simple random sampling from a complete sampling frame avoids systematic selection bias.

foundation.question_text: A university has $6000$ undergraduate students and $2000$ postgraduate students (total $8000$). A researcher takes a sample of $200$ undergraduates and $200$ postgraduates. Determine whether this sample is representative of the student body and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Undergraduates make up $75\%$ of the population but only $50\%$ of the sample, while postgraduates are over-represented.
Not representative; the strata are sampled in equal numbers rather than in proportion to population size.

foundation.question_text: A survey aims to determine the reading habits of all residents in a city by interviewing people at the central city library on a weekday afternoon. Identify which subgroup is under-represented.
foundation.solution_text:
People at work or school and non-readers are not present at the library on a weekday afternoon.
Not representative; working adults, students, and non-readers are under-represented.

foundation.question_text: A company has $400$ full-time staff and $100$ part-time staff (total $500$). A sample of $50$ staff contains $40$ full-time and $10$ part-time staff. Determine whether the sample is representative regarding employment type.
foundation.solution_text:
Full-time: $\frac{400}{500}=80\%$ of population, $\frac{40}{50}=80\%$ of sample.
Part-time: $\frac{100}{500}=20\%$ of population, $\frac{10}{50}=20\%$ of sample.
Representative; the sample proportions exactly match the population proportions.

development.question_text: A political polling organisation wants to survey voting intentions in an upcoming federal election. They conduct phone interviews using landline numbers listed in the White Pages. Explain why this sampling frame produces an unrepresentative sample.
development.solution_text:
Younger voters and households relying exclusively on mobile phones are absent from the landline directory.
Not representative; older residents who keep landlines are over-represented while mobile-only younger residents are excluded.

development.question_text:
A high school has the following enrolment numbers by year group:
$\begin{array}{lcccccc}\textbf{Year}&7&8&9&10&11&12\\ \hline \textbf{Students}&150&150&150&150&200&200\end{array}$
A survey on homework policy selects $20$ students from each of the $6$ year groups (total $120$). Explain why this sample does not represent the student population accurately.
development.solution_text:
Total population $=1000$ students. Year 11 and 12 make up $20\%$ each (should be 24 students each in a sample of 120), but only receive 20.
Years 7 to 10 make up $15\%$ each (should be 18 students each), but receive 20.
Not representative; senior students are under-represented relative to junior students.

development.question_text: An online shopping platform emails a customer satisfaction survey to all $50\,000$ customers who made a purchase last month. $800$ customers complete the survey. The company claims the sample represents all customers because every customer received the email. Evaluate this claim.
development.solution_text:
Although all customers were invited, only those who chose to respond are included in the sample.
Not representative; dissatisfied customers or highly enthusiastic customers are much more likely to respond than typical satisfied customers (voluntary response bias).

development.question_text: A regional council manages $12\,000$ rateable properties. Using the official rates register, the council selects every $40$th property after generating a random starting integer between $1$ and $40$, achieving a sample of $300$ properties. Evaluate whether this sample is representative.
development.solution_text:
The sampling frame is complete (all 12,000 properties), the starting point is randomised, and every property has an equal 1 in 40 chance of selection without periodicity bias.
Representative; systematic sampling across the complete register provides an unbiased sample.

development.question_text: A dental clinic wants to know how satisfied local residents are with local healthcare. The clinic distributes questionnaires to patients sitting in its waiting room. Identify the selection mechanism causing bias and state the effect on the survey conclusion.
development.solution_text:
Only individuals currently seeking dental care are surveyed, excluding healthy residents and those unable to afford private dental care.
Not representative; patients with active healthcare access are over-represented, leading to an over-estimation of healthcare satisfaction.

development.question_text: A factory produces $500\,000$ microchips daily. Quality control tests $10$ microchips chosen at random across the day and finds $0$ defects, concluding the entire daily batch has a $0\%$ defect rate. Explain why this conclusion is unjustified.
development.solution_text:
Testing only 10 chips out of 500,000 gives an extremely small sample fraction ($0.002\%$).
A defect rate of $1\%$ or $2\%$ (5000 to 10,000 defective chips) could easily yield zero defects in a sample of 10 by chance.
Not representative; sample size is too small to detect low-frequency defects reliably.

development.question_text: A hospital employs $300$ doctors, $600$ nurses, and $100$ administrative staff (total $1000$). A proposed representative sample of $100$ staff consists of $30$ doctors, $60$ nurses, and $10$ administrative staff. Verify mathematically whether this sample is representative by role.
development.solution_text:
Population ratios: Doctors $30\%$, Nurses $60\%$, Admin $10\%$.
Sample counts: Doctors $30$ ($30\%$), Nurses $60$ ($60\%$), Admin $10$ ($10\%$).
$\frac{30}{100}=0.30$, $\frac{60}{100}=0.60$, $\frac{10}{100}=0.10$.
Representative; each professional group is sampled in exact proportion to its size in the hospital population.

mastery.question_text: A social media influencer with $1\,000\,000$ followers runs a poll on their profile asking: 'Do you believe university degrees are worth the tuition cost?' $120\,000$ followers vote, with $85\%$ voting 'No'. The influencer asserts that $85\%$ of young Australians reject university degrees. Justify why this massive sample remains unrepresentative of young Australians.
mastery.solution_text:
1. The sampling frame is restricted to followers of that specific influencer, whose demographic and outlook may differ sharply from the general youth population.
2. The sample is self-selected (voluntary response), meaning followers with strong anti-university sentiment are more motivated to vote.
3. Having 120,000 responses simply multiplies the volunteer and selection bias without correcting the underlying lack of representativeness.

mastery.question_text: A national sports league has $320$ players across four divisions: Division 1 ($160$ players), Division 2 ($80$ players), Division 3 ($48$ players), and Division 4 ($32$ players). An athlete welfare committee selects a sample of $40$ players containing $14$ from Division 1, $12$ from Division 2, $9$ from Division 3, and $5$ from Division 4. Calculate the required proportional quota for each division, compare with the actual sample, and identify which division is most over-represented.
mastery.solution_text:
Sample fraction: $\frac{40}{320}=\frac{1}{8}$.
Required quotas: Division 1: $\frac{160}{8}=20$; Division 2: $\frac{80}{8}=10$; Division 3: $\frac{48}{8}=6$; Division 4: $\frac{32}{8}=4$.
Actual sample: Division 1 has $14$ (under by $6$), Division 2 has $12$ (over by $2$), Division 3 has $9$ (over by $3$), Division 4 has $5$ (over by $1$).
Not representative; Division 3 is the most over-represented division (over by $3$ players, or $+50\%$ above its quota).

mastery.question_text: A council wishes to determine community attitudes toward a proposed new park. It combines a complete municipal electoral roll with a stratified sampling plan by age group (18–34, 35–54, 55+) matching census proportions. Selected residents are contacted by mail and phone with multiple follow-ups, achieving an $85\%$ response rate. Justify two reasons why this sample is representative.
mastery.solution_text:
1. The complete electoral roll provides comprehensive coverage of all adult residents without excluding specific housing types or demographics.
2. Stratification guarantees proportional representation across key age brackets, and high response follow-up minimises non-response bias.
